entries.content_osis: <div eID="gen31318" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen31319" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31320" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen31319" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> In this chapter the prophet shows, under the type of hair, the judgments which God was about to execute on the inhabitants of Jerusalem by famine, sword, and dispersion, <reference osisRef="Eze.5.14">Eze 5:14</reference>. The type or allegory is then dropped, and God is introduced declaring in plain terms the vengeance that was coming on the whole nation which had proved so unworthy of those mercies with which they had hitherto been distinguished, <reference osisRef="Eze.5.5-Eze.5.17">Eze 5:5-17</reference>. <div eID="gen31321" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen31322" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> Take thee a sharp knife - Among the Israelites, and indeed among most ancient nations, there were very few edge-tools. The sword was the chief; and this was used as a knife, a razor, etc., according to its different length and sharpness. It is likely that only one kind of instrument is here intended; a knife or short sword, to be employed as a razor. <div eID="gen31323" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> Here is a new emblem produced, in order to mark out the coming evils. <div eID="gen31324" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> 1. The prophet represents the Jewish nation. <div eID="gen31325" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> 2. His hair, the people. <div eID="gen31326" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> 3. The razor, the Chaldeans. <div eID="gen31327" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> 4. The cutting the beard and hair, the calamities, sorrows, and disgrace coming upon the people. Cutting off the hair was a sign of mourning; see on <reference osisRef="Jer.45.5">Jer 45:5</reference> (note); <reference osisRef="Jer.48.37">Jer 48:37</reference> (note); and also a sign of great disgrace; see <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference>. <div eID="gen31328" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> 5. He is ordered to divide the hair, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.2">2Sam 10:2</reference>, into three equal parts, to intimate the different degrees and kinds of punishment which should fall upon the people. <div eID="gen31329" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> 6. The balances, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.1">2Sam 10:1</reference>, were to represent the Divine justice, and the exactness with which God's judgments should be distributed among the offenders. <div eID="gen31330" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> 7. This hair, divided into three parts, is to be disposed of thus: <div eID="gen31331" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> 1. A third part is to be burnt in the midst of the city, to show that so many should perish by famine and pestilence during the siege. <div eID="gen31332" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> 2. Another third part he was to cut in small portions about the city, (that figure which he had pourtrayed upon the brick), to signify those who should perish in different sorties, and in defending the walls. <div eID="gen31333" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> 3. And the remaining third part he was to scatter in the wind, to point out those who should be driven into captivity. And, <div eID="gen31334" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> 4. The sword following them was intended to show that their lives should be at the will of their captors, and that many of them should perish by the sword in their dispersions. <div eID="gen31335" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> 5. The few hairs which he was to take in his skirts, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.3">2Sam 10:3</reference>, was intended to represent those few Jews that should be left in the land under Gedaliah, after the taking of the city. <div eID="gen31336" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31337" type="x-p"/> 6. The throwing a part of these last into the fire, <reference osisRef="2Sam.10.4">2Sam 10:4</reference>, was intended to show the miseries that these suffered in Judea, in Egypt, and finally in their being also carried away into Babylon on the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar. See these transactions particularly pointed out in the notes on Jeremiah, chapters 40, 41, 42. Some think that this prophecy may refer to the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus Epiphanes.
entries.content_plain: Introduction In this chapter the prophet shows, under the type of hair, the judgments which God was about to execute on the inhabitants of Jerusalem by famine, sword, and dispersion, Eze 5:14 . The type or allegory is then dropped, and God is introduced declaring in plain terms the vengeance that was coming on the whole nation which had proved so unworthy of those mercies with which they had hitherto been distinguished, Eze 5:5-17 . Verse 1 Take thee a sharp knife - Among the Israelites, and indeed among most ancient nations, there were very few edge-tools. The sword was the chief; and this was used as a knife, a razor, etc., according to its different length and sharpness. It is likely that only one kind of instrument is here intended; a knife or short sword, to be employed as a razor. Here is a new emblem produced, in order to mark out the coming evils. 1. The prophet represents the Jewish nation. 2. His hair, the people. 3. The razor, the Chaldeans. 4. The cutting the beard and hair, the calamities, sorrows, and disgrace coming upon the people. Cutting off the hair was a sign of mourning; see on Jer 45:5 (note); Jer 48:37 (note); and also a sign of great disgrace; see 2Sam 10:4 . 5. He is ordered to divide the hair, 2Sam 10:2 , into three equal parts, to intimate the different degrees and kinds of punishment which should fall upon the people. 6. The balances, 2Sam 10:1 , were to represent the Divine justice, and the exactness with which God's judgments should be distributed among the offenders. 7. This hair, divided into three parts, is to be disposed of thus: 1. A third part is to be burnt in the midst of the city, to show that so many should perish by famine and pestilence during the siege. 2. Another third part he was to cut in small portions about the city, (that figure which he had pourtrayed upon the brick), to signify those who should perish in different sorties, and in defending the walls. 3. And the remaining third part he was to scatter in the wind, to point out those who should be driven into captivity. And, 4. The sword following them was intended to show that their lives should be at the will of their captors, and that many of them should perish by the sword in their dispersions. 5. The few hairs which he was to take in his skirts, 2Sam 10:3 , was intended to represent those few Jews that should be left in the land under Gedaliah, after the taking of the city. 6. The throwing a part of these last into the fire, 2Sam 10:4 , was intended to show the miseries that these suffered in Judea, in Egypt, and finally in their being also carried away into Babylon on the conquest of Egypt by Nebuchadnezzar. See these transactions particularly pointed out in the notes on Jeremiah, chapters 40, 41, 42. Some think that this prophecy may refer to the persecution of the Jews by Antiochus Epiphanes.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen31337" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31338" type="x-p"/> This is Jerusalem: I have set it in the midst of the nations - I have made this city the most eminent and the most illustrious in the world. Some think that these words refer to its geographical situation, as being equally in the center of the habitable world. But any point on a globe is its center, no matter where laid down; and it would not be difficult to show that even this literal sense is tolerably correct. But the point which is the center of the greatest portion of land that can be exhibited on one hemisphere is the capital of the British empire. See my Sermon on the universal spread of the Gospel.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen31338" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31339" type="x-p"/> She hath changed my judgments - God shows the reason why he deals with Jerusalem in greater severity than with the surrounding nations; because she was more wicked than they. Bad and idolatrous as they were, they had a greater degree of morality among them than the Jews had. Having fallen from the true God, they became more abominable than others in proportion to the height, eminence, and glory from which they had fallen. This is the common case of backsliders; they frequently, in their fall, become tenfold more the children of wrath than they were before.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen31339" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31340" type="x-p"/> I will do in thee that which I have not done - The destruction of Jerusalem by Nebuchadnezzar was one of the greatest calamities that ever fell on any nation or place before; and that by the Romans under Titus exceeded all that has taken place since. These two sackages of that city have no parallel in the history of mankind.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen31340" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31341" type="x-p"/> The fathers shall eat the sons - Though we have not this fact so particularly stated in history, yet we cannot doubt of it, considering the extremities to which they were reduced during the siege. The same is referred to by Jeremiah, <reference osisRef="Lam.4.10">Lam 4:10</reference>. Even the women, who were remarkable for kindness and humanity, boiled their own children, and ate them during the siege. <div eID="gen31341" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31342" type="x-p"/> Will I scatter into all the winds - Disperse you, by captivity, among all the nations of the earth.

entries.content_osis: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen31345" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen31346" type="x-p"/> So will I send upon you famine and evil beasts, and they shall bereave thee - Wild beasts always multiply in depopulated countries. In England, wolves abounded when the country was thinly peopled, it is now full of inhabitants, and there is not one wolf in the land. Nebuchadnezzar and his Chaldeans may be called here evil beasts. He is often compared to a lion, <reference osisRef="Jer.4.7">Jer 4:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.14">Dan 7:14</reference>; on account of the ravages made by him and his Chaldean armies.  <chapter eID="Ezek.5"/> <div eID="gen31346" type="x-p"/>
